plain_english: "What's the difference between me as a fool and you as a wise man?" The difference is everything. For a wise man, riches are servants. For a fool, riches are masters. You get used to wealth and cling to it as if someone promised it would be yours forever. But a wise man thinks most about poverty when he's surrounded by riches. No general trusts peace so much that he stops preparing for war. War may never come, but it's always possible. You get arrogant about your fine house, as if it could never burn down or collapse. Riches go to your head, as if they were safe from all danger and so vast that Fortune herself couldn't swallow them whole.
original_excerpt: "What difference, then, is there between me, who am a fool, and you, who are a wise man?" "All the difference in the world: for riches are slaves in the house of a wise man, but masters in that of a fool. You accustom yourself to them and cling to them as if somebody had promised that they should be yours for ever, but a wise man never thinks so much about poverty as when he is surrounded by riches. No general ever trusts so implicitly in the maintenance of peace as not to make himself ready for a war, which, though it may not actually be waged, has nevertheless been declared; you are rendered over-proud by a fine house, as though it could never be burned or fall down, and your heads are turned by riches as though they were beyond the reach of all dangers and were so great that Fortune has not sufficient strength to swallow them up.

plain_english: You sit there playing with your money, blind to the dangers ahead. You're like those primitive tribes under siege. They don't understand siege weapons, so they just watch the enemy build their war machines in the distance. They have no idea what's coming. That's exactly what you're doing. You sleep soundly on your pile of wealth, never thinking about all the disasters waiting to strike from every direction. Soon they'll strip you of everything valuable. But if you take riches away from a wise person, they still have everything that truly belongs to them. They live happily in the present and feel no fear about the future.
original_excerpt: You sit idly playing with your wealth and do not foresee the perils in store for it, as savages generally do when besieged, for, not understanding the use of siege artillery, they look on idly at the labours of the besiegers and do not understand the object of the machines which they are putting together at a distance: and this is exactly what happens to you: you go to sleep over your property, and never reflect how many misfortunes loom menacingly around you on all sides, and soon will plunder you of costly spoils, but if one takes away riches from the wise man, one leaves him still in possession of all that is his: for he lives happy in the present, and without fear for the future.

plain_english: The great Socrates, or anyone else with that same strength to resist life's pressures, would say: 'I have one firm rule — I won't change how I live just to please you. Go ahead and criticize me from every angle with your usual complaints. I won't think you're attacking me. You're just crying like babies.' This is what a wise person says. Their mind is free from flaws, so they can call out others — not because they hate them, but because they want to help them improve.
original_excerpt: The great Socrates, or any one else who had the same superiority to and power to withstand the things of this life, would say, 'I have no more fixed principle than that of not altering the course of my life to suit your prejudices: you may pour your accustomed talk upon me from all sides: I shall not think that you are abusing me, but that you are merely wailing like poor little babies.'" This is what the man will say who possesses wisdom, whose mind, being free from vices, bids him reproach others, not because he hates them, but in order to improve them:

plain_english: And he will add, "Your opinion hurts me — not for my sake, but for yours. When you hate what is good and attack virtue, you are giving up all hope of doing well yourself. You do me no harm. People don't hurt the gods when they tear down their altars. But it's clear you have evil intentions and would do harm if you could. I put up with your empty talk the same way Jupiter puts up with the silly stories poets tell about him. One poet gives him wings, another gives him horns. One makes him an adulterer who stays out all night. Another shows him being cruel to the gods or unfair to people. Another makes him a seducer who kidnaps noble young men by force — even his own relatives. Another calls him a father-killer who stole someone else's kingdom from his own father."
original_excerpt: and to this he will add, "Your opinion of me affects me with pain, not for my own sake but for yours, because to hate perfection and to assail virtue is in itself a resignation of all hope of doing well. You do me no harm; neither do men harm the gods when they overthrow their altars: but it is clear that your intention is an evil one and that you will wish to do harm even where you are not able. I bear with your prating in the same spirit in which Jupiter, best and greatest, bears with the idle tales of the poets, one of whom represents him with wings, another with horns, another as an adulterer staying out all night, another is dealing harshly with the gods, another as unjust to men, another as the seducer of noble youths whom he carries off by force, and those, too, his own relatives, another as a parricide and the conqueror of another's kingdom, and that his father's.

plain_english: The only result of such stories is that people feel less ashamed of their sins. They think it's okay because the gods supposedly do the same things. This doesn't hurt me personally, but for your own good, I urge you: respect virtue. Listen to those who have followed her for years. They shout that what they follow is powerful — and grows more powerful every day. Honor virtue as you would honor the gods. Honor her followers as you would honor priests. And when sacred writings are mentioned, _favete linguis_ — give us your silence. This phrase doesn't come from the word 'favor' like most people think. It commands silence so that sacred rituals can happen without being interrupted by unlucky words.
original_excerpt: The only result of such tales is that men feel less shame at committing sin if they believe the gods to be guilty of such actions. But although this conduct of yours does not hurt me, yet, for your own sakes, I advise you, respect virtue: believe those who having long followed her cry aloud that what they follow is a thing of might, and daily appears mightier. Reverence her as you would the gods, and reverence her followers as you would the priests of the gods: and whenever any mention of sacred writings is made, _favete linguis_, favour us with silence: this word is not derived, as most people imagine, from _favour_, but commands silence, that divine service may be performed without being interrupted by any words of evil omen.

plain_english: It's much more important that you be told to do this: whenever that oracle speaks, you should listen carefully and quietly. But look what actually happens. Someone shakes a rattle and claims a god told them to do it. Someone cuts their arms and shoulders with shallow wounds, making themselves bleed, and pretends to be holy. Someone crawls down the street on their knees, howling. An old man in linen robes comes out in broad daylight carrying a lamp and laurel branch, shouting that some god is angry. And what do you do? You gather around these people and hang on their every word. You feed off each other's amazement, all agreeing that these frauds must be divinely inspired.
original_excerpt: It is much more necessary that you should be ordered to do this, in order that whenever utterance is made by that oracle, you may listen to it with attention and in silence. Whenever any one beats a sistrum,[6] pretending to do so by divine command, any proficient in grazing his own skin covers his arms and shoulders with blood from light cuts, any one crawls on his knees howling along the street, or any old man clad in linen comes forth in daylight with a lamp and laurel branch and cries out that one of the gods is angry, you crowd round him and listen to his words, and each increases the other's wonderment by declaring him to be divinely inspired.
